name: Chloe Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to talk. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. So you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior associate in the corporate team at a large international firm, in their city office. Most of my work is due diligence, which means checking everything about a company before a client buys it: its contracts, its leases, any lawsuits. I'm in the firm's AI pilot group, so I use the AI tools every single day, mostly to read hundreds of contracts and flag the risky clauses. I like being the person who tries the new thing first and tells everyone whether it works.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Deal weeks, when everyone's up until two and the partner wants the report by seven. And my weak spot, honestly, is judgement: the tool finds 40 risky clauses and I'm still not great at knowing which three the client actually cares about. My supervising associate, Marcus, keeps telling me to think like the buyer. At home it's me and Ravi, my partner, who's a software developer at a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but overhyped, which is what our pilot group has been finding anyway. I'd probably write a short post about what actually worked in our pilot and what didn't. It would be practical, not preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm in a good spot. I'm already faster than most juniors because I use the tools well, and nothing radical changes, so my job and pay are safe. The only pressure is my own judgement, which is the bit I have to fix anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the pilot group and push the firm to use the tools on every diligence job, not just the big ones. I'd ask Marcus to let me write the summary section of the reports, so I practise judgement, not just finding things. And I'd keep putting £400 a month into an index fund, because our rent is fine and we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit flat. I like a challenge, so this one's almost boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainees who do the first-pass review by hand. If the plain tools do that, the firm might hire fewer of them next year. Fewer trainees would mean fewer people learning the job the way I did. I'd worry about the trainees, not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Ravi see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi would be relieved, honestly, because coding tools were scaring his team. We'd probably go out for dinner and joke about all the doom we read. Then we'd both go back to normal.

say: The tools are **useful but overhyped**, as our pilot found.
I'd post a **practical** note on what worked and what didn't.
think: I'm in a **good spot** because I already use the tools well.
My only real pressure is my own **judgement**.
do: Push the firm to use the tools on **every diligence job**.
Ask to write the **report summary** to practise judgement.
Keep investing **£400 a month** in an index fund.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit **flat**, because I like a challenge.
S0.quote: Fewer trainees would mean fewer people learning the job the way I did. I'd worry about the trainees, not about me.
fieldNote: She feels **secure** because she is already ahead on the tools.
She's honest that her weakness is **judgement**, not speed.
Her worry goes to **future trainees**, whose first-pass work is easy to trim.

steps.text: Stay in the firm's AI pilot group
Write the summary section of diligence reports for practice
Invest £400 a month in an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms that adapt early will be fine and the ones that don't will lose clients. At work I'd volunteer to train other juniors on the tools. Online I'd share what our team learned, because I think practical advice beats hand-wringing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think diligence teams get cut in half. Reading contracts and writing up risks is right there on the card, and it's most of my job. I'm probably safe because I'm the one running the tools, but the firm won't need as many people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move from the pilot group into a proper role setting up the firm's AI workflows for deals, even if it means less traditional lawyering. I'd build an automated checklist for each diligence job, so a junior only checks the flagged clauses. On the side, I'd offer weekend help to a couple of small law firms setting up their own AI tools, maybe £500 a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried. It's the kind of change I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer people like you. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia, the other junior in our team, still reads every page the old way. My colleague Mia is more careful than me, and the careful page-by-page way of working is exactly what the software replaces. Careful stops being an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would this change things for Ravi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi's job is on the same card, coding, so both of us would be in the same weather. We'd talk about not both being in jobs that shrink at the same rate. One of us might move to something steadier, but we'd decide that together.

say: Firms that **adapt early** will be fine; slow ones lose clients.
**Practical advice** beats hand-wringing, so I'd share what we learned.
think: I'm **probably safe** because I run the tools, but fewer people are needed.
do: Move into a role setting up the firm's **AI deal workflows**.
Build an **automated checklist** for each diligence job.
Help small firms set up AI tools for about **£500 a job**.
S1.quote: My colleague Mia is more careful than me, and the careful page-by-page way of working is exactly what the software replaces. Careful stops being an edge.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a **likely survivor** while her team halves.
She worries for a **more careful colleague**, which shows an honest view of who loses.
Both she and her partner are in **desk jobs**, which she's already thinking about.

steps.text: Build an automated diligence checklist that flags risky clauses
Ask to move into the firm's AI workflow role for deals
Help small law firms set up AI tools for about £500

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a proper national plan, not panic, and I'd say it calmly. At work I'd push the firm to tell staff honestly what happens next. I'd share sensible ideas online, like longer notice periods and paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one scares me, because Ravi and I are both screen workers. By 2028 the AI does diligence and coding better than either of us, and robots coming later doesn't help people at desks. I think one of us loses their job within a year, maybe both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the index fund and build cash instead, aiming for six months of both our costs by the end of next year. I'd look hard at work that needs a human signature or a human in the room, like regulatory roles or company secretary work, and apply early. We'd also talk seriously about moving somewhere cheaper, maybe near Ravi's parents, where rent is half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the optimist, so that's saying something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, almost nothing, because neither of us touches anything physical at work. It just means the jobs we might move into, things with your hands, are safe for three years longer. I've spent three years learning to be good with AI tools, and by 2028 the tools don't need me to be good with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been talking about getting married next year. We'd still do it, just smaller, at the registry office with lunch after, not the big thing. The money's better as a cushion.

say: We need a **national plan**, not panic, and I'd say it calmly.
Firms should tell staff **honestly** what happens next.
think: Ravi and I are **both screen workers**, so both jobs are at risk.
One of us **loses their job** within a year, maybe both.
do: Switch from the index fund to **cash savings** of **six months**.
Apply early for **regulatory** or **company secretary** roles.
Consider **moving near Ravi's parents**, where rent is half.
S2.quote: I've spent three years learning to be good with AI tools, and by 2028 the tools don't need me to be good with them.
fieldNote: The **two-earner** risk drives her mood: both she and her partner do **desk work**.
She shifts from investing to **cash** and from law to roles needing a **human signature**.
Wedding plans **shrink**, a small but telling change.

steps.text: Swap index fund payments for cash savings
Apply for regulatory and company secretary roles
Look at renting near her partner's parents for half the rent
Have a small registry office wedding instead of a big one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd tell juniors to learn the tools and also pick a second skill. I'd sound fairly upbeat, and mostly I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to make one good move, but probably not two. My job as it is goes by about 2030, I'd guess. I'd want to be in a role that oversees AI decisions, like compliance at a regulated company, before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the index fund going but at half, £200 a month, and put the rest into cash. In the first year I'd do a compliance qualification, about £1,800, and start applying in year two. And I'd keep the weekend consulting for small firms, because it shows I can do more than one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a focused way. I'd have a plan on one page and tick things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ravi do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi would probably move into security work at the bank, the people who check the AI isn't doing anything dodgy. We've already talked about it. In five years I get one good career move, not two, so I'd make the move into compliance count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marcus if he asked about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marcus the truth, that I'll stay as long as the work's there, but I'm training for compliance. He'd probably respect that. He's doing the same, I think, he just hasn't said.

say: Five years is enough to **get ahead** if you start now.
Juniors should learn the tools and pick a **second skill**.
think: My job as it is **goes by 2030**.
Five years is time for **one good move**, not two.
do: Halve the index fund to **£200 a month** and build cash.
Take a **compliance qualification**, about £1,800, in the first year.
Keep the **weekend consulting** for small firms.
feel: **Anxious**, but **focused**, with a plan on one page.
S3.quote: In five years I get one good career move, not two, so I'd make the move into compliance count.
fieldNote: She expects her current role to **end by 2030** but feels in control.
Her **compliance** plan has a cost and a timeline.
She and her partner are planning **in step**, both towards oversight roles.

steps.text: Take a compliance qualification costing about £1,800
Cut the index fund to £200 and save the rest as cash
Keep doing weekend AI setups for small law firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and anyone who panics now is wasting energy. At work I'd keep leading on the tools. Online I'd be the annoying person posting reading lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well for five or six years, because people like me are needed to run the change. After that I'm not sure, but I'd be in my mid-thirties with savings and a track record. My job looks safe for the next few years, which is about as far as I plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep investing £400 a month and keep my role in the pilot. I'd go for a promotion to senior associate on the strength of the AI work, around 2029. And I'd plan a move into a compliance or legal operations role a couple of years before 2036, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's on my mind, but mostly as a puzzle to solve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep investing. Isn't that risky if AGI changes everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If AI makes companies far more productive, I want to own a slice of those companies, not just work for them. That's my hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, around 2030, which would be before the big change. Ravi and I would want a bit more saved first. But I wouldn't let a date ten years off stop us.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, and panicking wastes **energy**.
I'd keep **leading on the tools** at work.
think: I'd do well for **five or six years** while firms need people to run the change.
My job looks **safe** for the next few years.
do: Keep investing **£400 a month** and stay in the pilot.
Go for **senior associate** around **2029** on the AI work.
Move into **legal operations** a couple of years before 2036.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly it feels like a **puzzle** to solve.
S4.quote: If AI makes companies far more productive, I want to own a slice of those companies, not just work for them.
fieldNote: She sees **investing** in AI-driven companies as a personal hedge.
With ten years her job feels **safe for now**, and she plans a **promotion**.

steps.text: Keep investing £400 a month in an index fund
Move into legal operations a few years before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Ravi and I would both be hit at once. What would help is clear notice from employers, at least a year, and paid retraining that's actually linked to real jobs. Some support for households where both earners are in the same boat would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. My partner Ravi writes code and I review contracts, and the AI does both. Two desk jobs in one flat is a risk I never thought about until now. Nobody talks about that risk in a household.

headlineQuote: My partner Ravi writes code and I review contracts, and the AI does both. Two desk jobs in one flat is a risk I never thought about until now.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** corporate junior at a **large international firm**, in the AI pilot group.
She's an **early adopter** whose weak spot is **judgement**, not speed.
She stays calm until AGI by 2028, when she and her partner both face **job loss**.
Her plans move from **investing** to cash, **compliance** training and a smaller wedding.
She sees the change as a **puzzle** when there's time, and a threat when there isn't.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both earners in desk jobs hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: At least a **year's notice** and **paid retraining** tied to real jobs.
Support for **two-earner households** caught in the same change.
